utterances.text: I stated that it was not an action there, in view of the position of the unit, the sector where the unit was. There was anti-armour artillery. It cannot move unless it is pulled. It performed the action together with MUP forces to crush the terrorists by taking up positions and blocking from the northern side of the village from their combat positions, and that implies a joint action.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you said that's a document of the Pristina Corps, you're referring of course to the "zapovest" or "odluka," the decision or the order, Dubrava, are you not?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't mean the Dubrava decision. I mean that this is a document of the corps command. I don't recognise it as my document. I see that the heading there is "status and activities of the units of the corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Who planned and authorised Dubrava, since you seem to know the details of what it entailed? Was it subject of an "odluka" map, identifying both VJ and MUP forces and their assignments?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that there was a particular plan, but if I remember well the case was that the terrorists attacked outside Dubrava village and the anti-terrorist action pushed them back. We relied on our intercommunication, and that was visible on the ground. The unit immediately took up their positions for defence and blocked the terrorist forces, disabling them from getting into position, and that was practically coordinated action with MUP forces in destroying the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... any losses you record 25 terrorists were liquidated in the carrying out of Dubrava action, and I believe it says there by the 243rd Brigade, and that's in the next -- the bottom -- we have to scroll down a little bit further "Gubici neprijatelja" 2.7. The subheading is visible on the bottom of the screen but the text of the actual report is not visible, so we need to scroll down the exhibit in e-court.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, you mean 2.7, yes, losses of the enemy. They are mixed in among units. It reads: "There is reliable information that 36 terrorists were liquidated: Namely, nine in the sector of Novoselskih Stanovi and Lipske mountain; 25 in the course of executing 'Dubrava' action (243rd Motorised Brigade), one in attempting to infiltrate himself into the sector of 'Deva', and one in the area of Budakovo village (east of Suva Reka by 6 kilometres). "In the course of performing 'Dubrava' action, the units of the 243rd Motorised Brigade seized six rifles, one machine-gun, one SnP with a muffler, two pistols, five hand-held rocket-launchers, six rounds for a recoilless gun, 300 rounds of various ammunition, and one Motorola device 210."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I apologise for pausing. I have to wait for the transcript to catch up with us from time to time. And now, having read this, would you -- are you better refreshed and better able to answer the question that you answered yesterday -- on Friday for Judge Bonomy when talking about the discovery of weapons and saying that you didn't know of any casualties in this area. Is it any clearer from here now that the Dubrava action, a legitimate anti-terrorist action undertaken by your forces and the MUP, resulted in your forces finding the weapons and disposing of 25 terrorists; that is to say that they actively participated in this legitimate action against criminal terrorist elements and had this effect on the criminal terrorist elements?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have stated that we did not get the number of casualties. There are -- there is rough terrain between us and the location, and we only later collected the weapons and we identified the casualties together with the MUP. Our data had to be merged, it had to be identified in one list, the man and the weapon, regardless of whether the body was found by the MUP or by us. This is the report that later went up towards the army, along the army line, towards General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the communication and reporting regime, as part of the reporting structure between the MUP forces in the field and your command units, worked well during the course of these legitimate anti-terrorist actions conducted in this region in 1999?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communications were sometimes difficult because of the well-known NATO campaign, because the repeaters were destroyed. But in most cases, most of the time, communications at short distance worked fine, especially between me and the chief of SUP, we had a constant exchange through Motorola devices. We exchanged frequencies and we communicated several times a day whenever a problem arose on the ground. Sometimes it was me asking his assistance, sometimes the other way round, but we communicated directly and we verified that information that we exchanged on lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now I'd like to move to Stagovo. As you heard, I'm trying to move through these areas of your testimony as efficiently as possible. Now, just so we can be clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's still your -- you're still maintaining the position here that the 25 casualties were casualties of the VJ, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm inquiring, and I believe he said that -- I'm taking his answer as he doesn't know which part were VJ and which part were MUP. So I'm asking questions and I'm guided by his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, as long as you weren't anticipating that I had agreed with you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Stagovo, general, at transcript page 18931, line 21 through 23, you stated that the VJ never set foot near the vicinity of this village or encircled it. At transcript page 18932, lines 20 through 21 you state members of the brigade never entered Stagovo and later say that the police controlled the terrain. I would like to call-up Exhibit 4D270, one for which I hope there will not be an issue of disclosure, as it was used in direct examination. And as that comes up, General, I'll ask you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for clarity, 4D270 was not used in direct examination. It was announced subsequently as well, and I want to emphasise that this is the third document that Mr. Ivetic is going to use, although he said he was using only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... If it was disclosed this is the one that was going to be used in direct examination because that's the notation I have. I apologise if it wasn't used, if Your Honours might recall, I was outside of court attending to other matters on Friday before assuming this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The objection is taken on the same basis as the last time, and we will allow the questioning to continue on this document on the same basis as in relation to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to this exhibit, and this one I think we have an English translation, General, so we won't have to read portions of it, but if I can direct your attention to section 2.1, which is at the bottom of the first page in both versions it would appear, and specifically in the B/C/S the sixth line seems to state that a part of the 243rd Motorised Brigade on 24 March 1999 executed a blockade of the villages of Runjevo and Stagovo and crushed the STS forces in these villages. Now, General, albeit I don't have military training as such, but common logic would seem to dictate that you must at least approach a village and perhaps encircle it in order to execute a blockade, and definitely some offensive measures must be taken to crush the STS forces therein. How can you reconcile this report of the 3rd Army dated the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, at that time terrorist forces attacked part of the MUP forces in Kacanik. There was six or seven casualties, hit from a hand-held launcher, and then the MUP forces pushed back these forces via Runjevo and Stagovo in a legitimate action, searching for the terrorists. Immediately after the beginning of this action, my unit was the closest to the area, close to old Kacanik, that's one kilometre away from Stagovo village. Don't forget that there is Nerodimka river in between and it's a swampy area, you can see it on the map. From the western side, that is, to the right of the Nerodimka river and north of Kamena Glava, we were located and we suffered constant attacks from terrorists. The army didn't use vehicles because we had self-propelled vehicles and they couldn't enter even if they had wanted to. And if you look at the configuration of the terrain, not a single combat vehicle, except a light one, can enter. We suffered constant attacks from Stagovo village, especially at night. When I say "from the sector," I don't mean from the village itself; I mean the features to the north and to the west of Stagovo village, nameless elevations from which fire was opened on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you differentiate from the actual village itself I see. Can we turn to page 3 of the Serbian original copy -- Serbian version of this document. It's at the top on the English -- my notes say it's on page 3 but I don't know the position of the document. But let me try it this way and it will be hopefully clear so we will be on the same page. General, as part of this combat report, I see the third bullet point on page 3 in the Serbian says -- in B/C/S, I apologise to the translators. [Interpretation] "In the course of the action in Runjevo and Stagovo villages, units of the 243rd Motorised Brigade liquidated five terrorists." [In English] General, this seems to indicate that the VJ forces in carrying out their legitimate anti-terrorist tasks actually engaged the criminal terrorist forces in the villages of Runjevo and Stagovo, according to my understanding of this passage. Does that refresh your recollection perhaps?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that they never opened fire on Runjevo or Stagovo village, only in combat with terrorists, that's one thing. Second, this date reminds me that we also suffered losses, one of our soldiers got killed while in his position by these terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, then, to complete the picture I'll call up 6D1313, which is the document that I had previously indicated would be coming up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But just before you go to that -- The five terrorists who were killed, are you saying that they were killed in the villages of Runjevo and Stagovo, as the report seems to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right. It seems from what is written they were in the villages, but they were actually in their positions on the mountain. And one of my soldiers got killed in combat in that sector, and in the same sector those five dead terrorists were found. That's north from Stagovo, maybe 700, 800 metres, perhaps a whole kilometre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, to complete the picture, 6D1313, which is the post-combat report of the Pristina Corps for the 22nd of May, 1999, strictly confidential 692/1-57. And indeed, according to my notes, on the second page in the B/C/S -- although, now I see it on the screen, it looks like it's just the B/C/S. The second page of the B/C/S, the last bullet point from the top, General, does it -- it reiterates that the five terrorists were killed by your forces in their legitimate action against the STS in the villages themselves, and the third paragraph from the bottom gives the precise time when your forces undertook the blockade of these villages and crushed the STS in these villages. And if we were to go the full length, the next page talks about one soldier who died as a result of this VJ action. So do you -- do you concede that, in fact, your earlier testimony that the VJ never approached these villages and that the MUP controlled the entire territory there was not entirely the full picture of this very complicated, chaotic situation, where both forces were involved in the legitimate struggle against the criminal elements of the STS?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not deny that we were engaged in combat with Siptar terrorist forces. We did engage in combat and we had losses. But as for entry into villages, shelling the villages, and search of civilians, that was not done in one single village anywhere in the area of responsibility of the brigade, not in a single village, because we were not authorised to do that, we had no right. We had several orders from the corps command, and my own orders prohibiting entry into villages, conducting searches, checking identity papers, and all the other activities that were in the purview of the MUP, that is the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I have to keep switching between the screens to try and get the transcript and the exhibit up. It seems like you're still a little bit unsure of whether your forces actually engaged the enemy in the village. If I can look at the fourth paragraph from the bottom of this document, sir, that's the part that I summarized for you. I'll read it to you in the Serbian to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, just let the General read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, could you read the fourth paragraph from the bottom that starts "u vremenu od 6" --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the time-frame from 6.00 to 1800 hours on the 21st of May part of the forces of the 243rd Motorised Brigade executed a blockade of villages Runjevo and Stagovo and crushed the Siptar terrorist forces in the said villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we have an issue here the document and the general just read -- said crushed the STS in the aforementioned villages. I think if the translators can confirm that for me, I can make my question to the General and at least conclude this point and move on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In the said villages, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have to go to the right channel to hear that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, does this refresh your recollection of whether you engaged the enemy criminal elements of the STS in the village of Stagovo and Runjevo, as it states here even for a period from 6.00 in the morning until 6.00 at night?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time is probably correct. Let me just remind you that this is not an original document from the brigade, it's from the corps command. The unit was engaged in combat against terrorists in the area of Stagovo village north of Runjevo. That means in the area of the village, not in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, General, how do you crush terrorist forces in the village without engaging them in the village?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am replying to the question you asked. You are now asking a different question that is not related to this. The army did not enter villages to combat terrorists. The army blocked from the north across Nerodimka river and from there targeted positions of the terrorist forces that were north of Stagovo. It did not target inside Stagovo and it did not enter into the village to conduct searches for these terrorist forces, and MUP didn't either. After destroying the terrorists, the MUP searched the terrain and pursued the fleeing terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know -- I have the wrong document on the screen, that would explain it. If we could go to page 5 of this exhibit -- actually, the bottom of page 4, first, and section 8 or item 8. The first bullet point under section 8, General, could you read that for us.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read it, but I don't recognise whose document this is so it practically means nothing. It's an excerpt from a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's the same document we've looked at, 1313, the Pristina Corps combat report. I can give you the information if it will assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please just read that sentence aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Continue the actions that had been started in searching the terrain and preparing forthcoming actions, in keeping with the decision of the Pristina Corps commander. "Continue engineering activities in building defence areas."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... including your region, the VJ conducted searches of the terrain as well, again in conjunction with, in cooperation, with the MUP in carrying out their legal and legitimate assignments?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VJ was authorised to search the terrain in the defence areas of the units at the positions. Furthermore, the units which were in the border belt could also do that. So it was only in those two cases that they could search the terrain. That had to be done also according to the Rules of Combat when the units were moving from one position to another and taking up new positions. Before the unit arrived, they would send a part of their forces to search the terrain and thus make it possible for the unit to take up its positions. It was prohibited for a unit to take up any combat position unless the terrain had been checked for security, that means unless it had been searched and secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could move on to Belanica, the last inhabited village in this municipality that I want to discuss with you before moving on to other issues. With respect to Belanica, I believe you stated at page 18952 of the transcript, the last ten lines, that your troops were not involved and did not enter the village, and you described in some detail the triage and searches conducted in the village to identify terrorists by the MUP. Now, at transcript page 18953, lines 16 through 17, you, in fact, deny that your units had any contact with the civilians from Belanica. How is it then that you knew with such precision what was going on in the town? Was it, again, a case of the MUP forces operating as part of a joint, legitimate anti-terrorist action pursuant to a "zapovest," order or decision, of the Pristina Corps authorised by you -- pardon me, undertaken by your units and the MUP units in the field that the MUP was reporting through the reporting system what was going on in Belanica, or did you also have units in Belanica?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. There were many questions there, more than ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... because I only have a handful of questions left so I think I can do it and not waste too much time. First of all, your unit's involvement in the Malisevo-Suva Reka region around Belanica that you described in your direct examination were performed on the basis of a "zapovest" that you received from the Pristina Corps command. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. The "zapovest," the order, of the corps commander was complied with, and I issued my own order in compliance with that and then the subordinate units issued their own orders in compliance with my order.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have a clear and present recollection of the specific tasks for your units from that "zapovest," or do you need to have your recollection refreshed by looking at the document that I believe is the "zapovest" you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the document, but I would like to have it shown here because of the lapse of time. But the main intention was for the road from Suva Reka via Blace, Malisevo, and so on, be deblocked because that road had been cut off completely. And in the Malisevo area in that period, according to our information, there were about three brigades of terrorists. If I recall correctly, the aim was to support the MUP forces in routing the terrorist forces which were blocking the road with various barricades, fortifications, and land-mines, to make sure that the road was constantly passable from Dulje to Suva Reka and Malisevo, and to keep the road under the control of the legal and legitimate authorities. I think that was the task, to the best of my recollection, in the routing of these terrorist forces on that axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to the document in a second, but the road that was secured from Suva Reka to Malisevo, one had to pass through Belanica on that road, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one does have to pass through Belanica. It remains to the right and then one goes on to Malisevo. So you don't actually pass through the village, you pass by the village, going towards Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can pull up P1969, since the General requested the document that I believe is the "zapovest" for this action?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, this that's going to come up is a "zapovest," order, of the -- it says in the title "the Joint Command," which General Lazarevic testified I think in fact originated from the Pristina Corps. Do you recall receiving such a document and operating under such a "zapovest" for purposes of carrying out the activities that you've described in and around Malisevo and Belanica?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we zoom-in, please? Yes, this is one of the documents I received from the commander of the Pristina Corps; it was accompanied by a map, plans of communications, and all the various kinds of security, rear, and so on, security and so on. This is one of the documents pertaining to the manner of execution of this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to -- I believe it's the third page at section 5.3, I think I can short-circuit looking at the rest of the document if we focus on that. It should be the next page, 5.3, part 3. If we can look at the -- under 5.3, the section of assignments that is -- that would be the second -- I'm getting some feedback. The paragraph in the middle of that assignment under 5.3, and that starts off: "Extend the attacks, destroy the remaining STS along the directions of attack, and as the next assignment, take control of the line: Village of Belanica- village of Banja- village of Kravosarija- village of Pagarusa." Isn't it correct that your units were undertaking these tasks as part of the legitimate, joint, concerted action against the criminal STS, including in Belanica?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that my units, in compliance with decision of the corps commander, supporting the MUP forces in routing the Siptar terrorist forces on this axis were supposed to come out on to the line: Belanica, Banja, Kravosarija to the right, and Pagarusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have 6D231 up, this is a map of Suva Reka municipality, and I would ask so we can see what these names mean in geographic terms. I have General mark some of these locations on the map to demonstrate the oral testimony that he's given and that the document sets forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document has not been announced in advance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you objecting to it, Mr. Cepic? I mean, are you objecting to a map being shown for some reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not a problem to show the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, with the help of the usher, I think we can use the mechanical pen there, electronic pen to have you indicate for us the progression of your forces, as foreseen by this decision or order, "zapovest," I guess it's an order.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's something wrong in the interpretation -- or the translation. It can't be "napredak," progress, it's task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you clarify your question for Mr. Jelic, please, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was progress in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was "progress."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you indicate for us the task of your forces as foreseen by this decision and based upon your knowledge of how they effectuated this decision on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's that line meant to signify, Mr. Jelic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My unit was at Dulje. Its task was to go from the village of Blace, which I'm indicating here, it was at Dulje. Its task was to support the MUP forces from the village of Blace on the road leading from Suva Reka, via the village of Dulje, and further on towards Malisevo. So from here it had the obligation to provide support along this axis, that is, along the road. And to the best of my recollection, the task was to reach Malisevo, but because there was strong terrorist forces there, three to four brigades, the units stopped. And the last position they held while providing support was here, near the village of Tumicina and in front of the village of Pagarusa, and I'll mark it here like this. Those are the two axes along which they went to rout the terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what does the line you first put on the map represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentleman wanted to know what the task was, how far our forces were supposed to go in routing the terrorist organizations along that axis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, isn't it a fact that the assignment for your troops was to go further towards Malisevo, beyond this point that you have discussed near -- I believe it's the Kosturic-Belanica line?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look at the order I read where it says "come out on the Belanica-Banja-Pagarusa line," that's what I read out, Belanica, Banja, Pagarusa. I can't recall exactly what it says, but that's the line they were supposed to reach; however, there were very strong terrorist forces there. There was fierce fighting from Malisevo towards Belanica Guncat and the north eastern part, the villages of Simic, Petrovic, and further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's my point, sir, if you look on the map Banja, Guncat are further north up towards Malisevo on the map. Could you draw the line and mark it A of the planned extent of your force's penetration towards Malisevo in carrying out the tasks and assignments specified in the "zapovest" that we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That question's been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the map is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's marked on the map where the unit was supposed to get to and where they actually got to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the "zapovest" says Banja which is not on the area marked on the map, that's up further north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. That's something you can argue about later. Let's get on with this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if the line was supposed to extend to the Banja-Belanica line, which would be north -- I guess it would be north-west of the line that you've drawn slightly?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but one always marks below the name of the village, not above it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you actually passed Belanica in practice on the terrain in the course of events; isn't that correct then?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know on what basis you assume that. I told you where the task was and up to where the task was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you -- did you actually carry out to completion the tasks contained in the "zapovest"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, why do you not accept that the witness has answered the question where the troops reached?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's save this exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you don't like it, I'm afraid you'll just need to deal with it later. The evidence is the evidence and you have to make your submissions later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll let the documents make the submissions for me. If we can save this for an IC number for whatever it's worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to 4D371.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC144, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Once this exhibit comes up ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 4D371 is a document I don't see on any list. It may be an oversight on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Hopefully we'll see the document so I can make reference to it and see. I don't have a hard copy in front of me for some reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's on the screen now apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh. It's not updating on my personal screen, I have to look on the ... Oh, now it's on the screen. Well, this is a -- I, again, don't know if it's -- if it was part of the amended list or not. I did not -- I thought the last one that I had on that amended list was 6D1313. It's an exhibit that may even have been -- I don't know if it's been used before or not, but in any event it's relevant. It goes towards the activities in question in Belanica. It's from the command of the Pristina Corps. I doubt there can be an issue of authenticity, since it was tendered by one of the military defendants -- on their lists at least if it hasn't been already tendered or evidenced. I'm going to have just one question relative to this to ask him to explain whether, in fact, he completed his assignments according to the "zapovest" because this is a report about the progress of his units in relation to the "zapovest."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not on a list; why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't have an answer for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And for what it's worth, it's already exhibited in the case and therefore any submissions you want to make about it you can make in due course. It was exhibited on the 25th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That brings me to my last topic for discussion. General, in the course of your direct examination you stated there had never been any resubordination of the MUP to the VJ. What tangible efforts were undertaken by you to try and effectuate resubordination or any problems arising therefrom?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order from the corps commander to me was that the Urosevac MUP should be resubordinated to my brigade, but this was never implemented. I tried on several occasions with the chief of the Urosevac SUP, I contacted him, we discussed the topic, and he said that he did not have any order from his staff for resubordination. And there was nothing left for me to do as commander but to report on this to my superior, the corps commander. I continued to ask that he do this, but quite rightly, he did not dare do such a thing without first receiving the task from his own staff. So he was never resubordinated, even though several attempts were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you said the MUP in Urosevac. Am I correct that there were no manoeuvre or territorial PJP detachments present in your zone of responsibility, that the sole units there were the SUPs and OUPs and the local PJP elements within those SUPs and OUPs?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Urosevac SUP had several OUPs, but he'll probably be able to explain that better than me. It was not a unit of mine for me to explain here, but there was the Urosevac SUP which had several stations from Kacanik to Strpce, and he managed them and he had his own units which he established; but in what way and following what orders, that's something I don't have access to. But the fact is he did have some units, whether they were permanent or temporary, I don't know, but I think they were temporary units he established for particular activities. These units were never part of my combat units in my areas of responsibility and they were never resubordinated to my units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, which units did you expect to resubordinate to you? Surely you did not expect the SUP and the chief of the SUP to be resubordinated to you in the strictest military sense, did you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly I didn't write that order. I certainly didn't ask for that. There was an explanation. I don't need a passport department or an ID card department. What I needed was a squad that could carry out action on the ground. I didn't need office clerks. There was an order I think in May that dealt with that, but it actually never came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You said you needed a "borbena odeljenja" would that be a combat office within the SUP? Is that how I'm to understand your testimony as to who you thought needed to be resubordinated? Are you saying that the -- an entire division of the SUP of Urosevac was to be subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I think we received a very clear answer to this question. It's been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't see what the answer is, Mr. Cepic. The question is endeavouring to find out clearly who it was that Mr. Jelic was seeking to have subordinated to him, and I don't see an answer to that question. Can you help us, Mr. Jelic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try. At a meeting with the chief of the SUP, the intention was to resubordinate combat units, territorial units on the territory who were controlling the territory and able to carry out combat activities. As for other parts of the MUP, offices and staffs, we really didn't need that. We couldn't deal with that, it's not our profession, and we are not trained to carry out those activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, did the lack of resubordination get reported in your combat reports that were sent to the command of the Pristina Corps, either regular or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The resubordination never reached him; my reports that went to the corps commander confirmed that, and the SUP chief confirmed that in a statement he made before this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you ever unable to carry out any anti-terrorist action due to a refusal on the part of the police to resubordinate; and if so, where is that reflected in your combat reports?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were two counter-terrorist actions in the sector if I'm not mistaken, on the Crnoljevo, or rather, Dulje axis, now I'm not sure whether it went to Blace. But I think that one unit, one MUP unit did not come on to this axis. We supported the forces that were already there, and they refused to carry out that task, but once they heard that the other units had already arrived they rejoined the MUP battle formation. I don't know which unit that was, but I do know that there was a unit on this axis because there were a number of activities there on this axis so I don't know the numerical designation of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the duration of the war, the concerted action and cooperation between yourself and the SUP of Urosevac and the policemen therein was successful, is that correct -- was without major problems?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make an addition to my previous answer. I reported to the Pristina Corps command about that MUP unit. My cooperation with the Urosevac MUP, or rather, the chief was extremely correct and professional. When combat actions were carried out, there were some problems but that only natural because such problems occurred even when our troops were the only ones engaged, in most cases, however, those problems were dealt with, they were resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Jelic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecution by Ms. Kravetz. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Jelic.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is this working? I don't have any volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it's working.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sorry. I had no sound in my headphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, I would like to begin by asking you some questions about the contacts you had with your corps commander, General Lazarevic, during the war. Did you have regular meetings with your corps commander in 1999 during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible to have regular meetings with the corps commander, as had been the usual practice, given the critical situation. But such meetings were held intermittently, in most cases they were held at the corps command post and the corps commander also visited the units very often, at least I can say that for my own brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And at those meetings, would other brigade commanders also be present to discuss the situation or would it just be a one-to-one meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those meetings were never held one on one, as far as I know. There would also be other people there, parts of the command, so elements from the corps command and the corps commander would have meetings with the subordinate commanders, the commanders of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how often would the corps commander come visit you at your command post?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's not a problem, but could you please give me the relevant time-period that you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm interested in the period during the war, as of March 1999.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the corps commander visited the units, not at the command post but units in the brigade three or four times, and twice we were visited by the army commander. I don't know whether the General Staff team also came, but for the most of the time the chief of the armoured and mechanised units administration in the General Staff, General Kovacevic, was present there at the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And at these meetings would you generally brief the corps commander about the activities that your units were undertaking at the time?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly there was discussion and briefings about the combat-readiness of units, problems, achievements, positive achievements, and problems and how to solve them in the units. These were the key issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Would you also have regular contact with brigade commanders of other brigades deployed in Kosovo at the time, during the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the principle of military subordination, we could not have contacts with the brigade commanders horizontally. Our relations were vertical, through the Pristina Corps command. But if units engaged in combat or if a decision is received, the adjacent units are listed on the maps. And we knew them and we were then supposed to ensure coordination among the units to -- to avoid any gaps in the lines, at the flanks, and that was our obligation as brigades positioned next to one another, to adjacent brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how was that coordination ensured in practice? Would there be a regular exchange of information of actions that you or other brigades were going to undertake?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify a bit. Coordination has to do with the adjacent units of the brigades at the border between the area of responsibility of one brigade and the area of responsibility of the other brigade, those units had to be completely linked in military parlance. Everybody has to know who does what and who is responsible for what at those adjacent points where the brigades touched upon each other. And as for any other actions, no reports were asked and no information was supposed to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You're saying no information was supposed to be exchanged between brigades, but how would you know what sort of action brigades were -- neighbouring with you would be undertaken? Would this be information that would come to you through the corps command?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, this kind of information pertaining particularly to combat engagements came from the corps command. We exchanged information only in those areas where two units were positioned next to each other, because in that way we relieved the chain of command. We made sure that the flow of information was faster, because otherwise there would be a bottleneck that would affect the operation of the units because the information had to go up to the corps command and if the corps command thought that something had to be done then they would issue an order to our adjacent unit, telling them what to do in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where was your command post located during the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My command post at the beginning of the war was in Duganovici. Since this post was discovered quite soon, the location was identified, we moved into several other locations, from Djeneral Jankovic to Dulje. So the command divided into several elements, in order to be able to provide assistance in the decision-making, to direct the units, and in order to lift the morale and to provide support to the commanders in those difficult circumstances. So the command actually split into three elements. This is something that is envisaged in the Rules of Service and this was done in compliance with those rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you would be mostly based at the command post? Would that be your location where you would be based generally?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a rule, this is called the command post. This is where the commander is, but it doesn't necessarily have to be so. But the major part of the command is located there and all the information flows into that location and all the orders for the subordinate units are issued from that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Would you also regularly tour your units in their zones of deployment?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in addition to the teams that toured the units from the corps command and upwards, we at the brigade command set up teams who would tour all the units in 15-day periods. They would also provide assistance. There were operations officers, logistics officers, the composition was geared in order to provide as much assistance for the work and life in the units as possible, given the circumstances. So in any given 15-day period, those teams would tour all the units in their positions. You have to bear in mind that this is 88 kilometres from the border of Macedonia and -- 88 kilometres from the border with Macedonia and 150 kilometres into the depth of the territory, a total of about 250 kilometres of front line, and the front line extended from Djeneral Jankovic all the way down to Belanica near Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I understand from your evidence here today that your subordinate units were duty-bound to report all their activities, regularly report their activities to you at the brigade command level.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, this is envisaged in the rules, and all the subordinates are obliged to report to their superiors about the situation in their units. But because of fierce fighting with the terrorist forces, the destruction of the repeater station, and constant air-strikes, several times during the day in any number of sectors, many of the communications equipment -- a lot of it was destroyed, so the communications were disrupted, sometimes for days, and sometimes we would have no idea of what was going on in a smaller unit somewhere far away for five or six days and the biggest problem was how to provide assistance down there, especially if they suffered any casualties. So the exercise of command was uninterrupted, but in difficult circumstances. We were trying to deal with that by dispatching liaison officers from the brigade to the subordinate units or the other way around, from the subordinate units to the brigade, and -- but sometimes the correspondence reached us too late.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think this is an appropriate moment for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one thing you might clarify, Mr. Jelic, before we adjourn. You gave two distances there, 88 kilometres and 150 kilometres. Can you tell us again what these related to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made a mistake. 88 kilometres with Macedonia and 150 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the answer, it's not clear -- the interpreter has been unable to hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The length of the front facing the Republic of Macedonia was 88 kilometres, and in the depth of the territory, about 70 kilometres, which gives a total of about 150 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break again. Could you leave the courtroom with the usher, and we'll resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, before the break we were talking about the issue of reporting from your subordinate units up to the brigade command level. Would you -- from the brigade command level would you send regular reports up to the corps command level during the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular reports to the corps command were sent almost through regular combat reports, but if necessary we would also send interim combat reports sometimes because the communication lines were disrupted, the exercise of command was made difficult both at the operational and the technical level, and the lines were down. Sometimes the delay would be a couple of days but all the reports would reach the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you kept your corps commander and his staff well informed about developments and actions taken in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that all the tasks, all the obligations in the area of responsibility of the brigade were reported to the corps command. No larger-scale task -- in no case were any large-scale tasks not reported to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And in addition to this obligation of reporting your activities, were all units from the battalion level up under the duty to keep a war diary once the state of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Battalion-level units, artillery battalion-level units, or other units of similar size were under an obligation to keep a war diary from the moment a state of war was declared until it was revoked. So from battalion level up, all the units have to have their war diary. It's an auxiliary document that assists in the exercise of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would it be correct to say that the purpose of this war diary was to record all actions taken by the units and all important events that took place each day? Was that the purpose of the war diary?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the format of the war diary, all the key events in the course of the day in that unit should be recorded in it, that's the format.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if anyone wanted to know what happened in your area of responsibility on a given day, they can turn to the war diary and they would find the information recorded there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, that is how it should be. I'm sure there were some minor omissions, but as a rule this is how it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, General, this war diary was a public document, accessible to anybody? That's what you are saying? Anybody could see it, do you mean that, even a man not of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The diary is one of the documents kept in the units at the battalion level and up. It cannot be a public document, accessible to everyone. It is made for the use of that command, the battalion, artillery battalion, and this is where it is kept. The battalion command does not have its operation organ, a large operations organ. Maybe there are three or four people. It's just one person keeping it there at the battalion command, and any -- it is not something that anyone can have access to, anyone, just an unknown person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, now that's clarified. One more clarification I would request you to make is that you stated that you reported things only pertaining to the activities of your units to the high command. I mean, that is the routine. But now you were confronting an extraordinary situation and there were so many other things going on besides the normal regimental tasks. Would you be reporting those to your high command as well or you kept to the old routine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usual routine was maintained before the aggression, but during the aggression those meetings were far more rare. But the reports came in more frequently. So during the day we reported to the corps commander about all the events, and we would also send in interim reports, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That has clarified the answer to her question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In -- we were just talking about the war diary. If I understand correctly, once you get a report from a subordinate unit you would enter -- at the brigade level I mean, you would enter a summary of the report in the war diary and then the report would be collated, to later be sent on to the command, corps command. Is that how it functioned?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, you're right. All the events that happened at the brigade level from all the units would be summarized, and then an analysis would be made and this was then sent to the Pristina Corps command from the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And that summary of the combat report sent by the unit would be entered in the war diary of the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those focal units that were summarized -- those -- this was supposed to be in the war diary, and once it was all processed it was supposed to be sent to the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall who kept the war diary for your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations officer is supposed to keep it in the brigade. I think it was kept by a major who was seconded from the command and staff school to assist us, I can't recall his last name, but I will, I will, that's for sure, because he was in the staff and he was one of the people who actually kept the war diary. I'm not sure about his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. No problem. During your testimony last week, last Friday, you told the Chamber that once the NATO bombing -- or right prior to the NATO bombing your unit left the barracks. You said that quite literally the barracks were deserted. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately before the aggression started, on D-Day, as we say in military parlance, all the units left the barracks where they had been, and they took up positions in their sectors. It didn't take an hour or two, it took some time, but all the materiel reserves had to be relocated and echeloned in the depth by the D-Day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you have told the Chamber now on a number of occasions that your units were never deployed in civilian facilities and that you never used any type of private or civilian buildings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian buildings or facilities were never used during the war. All the units were at their positions, and some elements used only state-owned or socially-owned facilities. So troops were not billeted and did not work in civilian buildings because units were on the front lines, in the woods, in the meadows, camouflaged. Only the infirmary was always in Urosevac, it was there all the time; it treated the wounded, the sick. And because it was next to the health care unit, it treated civilians, too, as did the health care centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And it is also your evidence that you never deployed any sort of military equipment in civilian facilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military equipment was never deployed in private homes, any private property. It was mostly in state-owned companies or socially-owned companies because that's one of the forms of ownership that we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have also told the Chamber now on a number of occasions during your testimony that your units never entered built-up areas and never entered villages in your zone of -- your area of responsibility. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My evidence is as follows: They never entered them for combat purposes, they never fought in built-up areas. They passed through a number of towns and villages, because roads pass through them and we didn't avoid those roads and after all, there was no need to do so. And on most occasions we didn't suffer any casualties in the built-up areas, so there was no need to avoid those roads, to construct new roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you're saying that your units were never located in any villages or in any built-up areas?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not located in villages, they were in their positions. They couldn't be in positions while in villages, otherwise they wouldn't be able to perform their main task.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P2021 up on the screen. I would like to show the witness page 5 in the B/C/S and it's also page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, General, as this exhibit is coming up, this is the war diary for your brigade. And I would like to show you an entry dated 29 March 1999, if we could have that up on the screen. I think it's the top part of the B/C/S page, and if I see the English it should be at the bottom of the page. Can you see that on your screen, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we enhance it a bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: As we seem to have lost the English, I'll read out the -- I think it's -- yeah, scroll up. The entry dated 29 March, the first line, if you can see that, it says: "Work on the dispersion of RMS continued," and there is an illegible passage, "in the barracks in deployment in houses and towns." Can you see that, General, there?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now if we go to the next page in the English and it's the same page on the B/C/S but we need to scroll down. Yes, I think that's it. It says: "The dispersion of RMS from the barracks," there is an illegible passage, "houses in the town continued." Have you had the chance to read it there on your screen?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: These two entries of the war diary of your brigade seem to indicate that there was use of houses in the town and deployment in houses in the town of your unit; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, judging by this here, looking at how it's written, you could make that conclusion. However, in town we had a large number of facilities, houses, like Bosko Cakic company, Sar company, where you cannot place ammunition. It's large-calibre ammunition, the size is very large. They don't fit -- such things don't fit into houses. 2.000 tonnes of explosive or shells cannot be placed in a house, it's absurd.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But these entries do indicate that there was deployment in houses in the town -- it's referring to the town of Urosevac, if you read earlier entries, there was deployment in private houses; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that munitions and explosive were not placed in any privately owned house. That would have been hazardous, not only because the army could lose them but also because there would be the danger of chaos and huge losses to the civilian population. Dozens of houses would be destroyed, could be destroyed, and a huge number of people could be killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So are you saying that explosives and ammunitions were not placed in privately owned houses, but that troops were deployed in private houses?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The reference here is to commodities, materiel stocks. The soldiers were not in town, the troops were outside town in their positions. If you could look at the report for that day or previous day that we sent to the corps command, you would find exact explanations where the munitions and explosives were stored. You would certainly not find a reference to them being stored in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can we look at the same page 6 in the B/C/S and it's page 6 also in the English, the same exhibit. It's in the top -- in the B/C/S it's the top part of the page, first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you see a reference there, General, to the command post and it says: "The command post was relocated from the," and there's an illegible passage, "club to the Amazona cafe." The Amazona cafe sounds like a private facility, private establishment; isn't that true, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it here, although it's very badly written, but the command was in the building of the club of the Army of Yugoslavia the beginning of the war, then it was divided and one part was located in the basement of that building - what's its name? I can't remember - anyway, they were in shelters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So how can you explain that there is an entry here in your war diary describing the location of the command post as being the Amazona cafe?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a decision from the corps commander, and according to that decision the command post is identified in Duganovici village. The command post never was in town and couldn't be in town because of the roads, because of the impact on units, and, quite simply, it couldn't be changed without special decision from the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you're basically telling me you can't really explain why this entry is -- exists in your -- in the war diary of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain this because this was written by somebody else. It's one of the auxiliary documents. The main document for all activities was the order from the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, General, you told us - and I just reminded you earlier - that the barracks were completely abandoned on 24th March, when the bombing began.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we can scroll up on that page, page 6 of the English, and it should be page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you see there, there's a reference to an attack on the barracks and there's an indication to casualties suffered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You should scroll down on the other page. It's at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, if the barracks were completely abandoned on 24th March, why is there an entry here in your war diary regarding casualties suffered during an attack on the barracks?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are the persons -- you see here, they are -- one is from the logistics, a cook, a food handler. They were wounded in the barracks. The barracks was abandoned but it was still a military installation. It was always secured by ambushes and patrols. They were secured from illegal entry so that what little remained would not be destroyed. That first attack on the barracks was on the 25th, the first -- the first bombs fell on the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you're saying the barracks weren't completely abandoned on 24th March due to the NATO bombings.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks was abandoned, but there was security on the outside so that there would be no unauthorised entry. There were guard posts and patrols. The guards were not inside, they were outside, because already on the 24th the barracks were targeted by air-strikes. There were just guards outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we move on in the same exhibit to page 71 of the English and it's page 59 of the B/C/S. This, Your Honours, is part of the same exhibit but it's the war diary of the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the same brigade. It's been uploaded in e-court as one exhibit because it's been provided to us as one single document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, do you see this is an entry dated 6 April 1999, and I'm going to read to you the paragraph under number 2 where it says "own forces." Do you see that on your screen?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The second line of that paragraph says: "The 2nd Mechanised Company has been relocated from the Korbulic sector to Smira villages. There were no losses on our side during the movement and conduct of operations." This is an example of deployment of troops in a village in your area of responsibility; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question, but if you read this passage it says that during the clearing of Smira village we encountered minor resistance which was crushed in movement and destroyed. This activity was performed in coordinated action with the units of PJP Gnjilane. The unit was located in Korbulic sector and in Smira village. That's all right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have told this Chamber on numerous occasions that your units never entered villages, and here with have an entry indicating that they were relocated from Korbulic to Smira village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was relocated from Korbulic sector to the area of Smira, not the village but the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have that part read I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- so that we get the clear language. You see the sentence, Mr. Jelic, that begins: "The 2nd Mechanised Company ..." Could you read that, please, read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The 2nd Mechanised Company was relocated from the area Korbulic into Smira village. During movement and performance of activities, there were no" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The language appears to refer to Smira village, which suggests that's a built-up area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but it means that the movement was from Korbulic area to village Smira. However, units take up positions in the area, not inside a village. It would simply be impossible inside a village, because to get into position means to place your artillery pieces somewhere. You cannot be on a street or inside a house. It would be absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can I show you another example from the war diary of the 2nd Mechanised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is page 79 of the English and 67 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is an entry dated 14th April 1999, and here again under number 2 "own forces" we have a section called "activities." Could you read that passage out to us right where it starts: "During the morning ..."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the course of the day -- in the morning, the 2nd Mechanised Company was relocated from the area of Smira village to Korbulic village. In the course of movement there were no problems. The mortar company was relocated to Samakovo area from Binac village, and then work was done on making obstacles and fortification of the sectors of the" -- you see, the writer mixes these two words "sector" and "village." He uses one and then the other interchangeably.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you're saying that this is a mistake in the entry and that this does not show that your units were actually deployed in built-up areas, in the village? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only my position. You can look on the map to see where those units were located, because it's impossible to place mortars and armoured personnel carriers on to a street or in a house, expecting an aggressor to advance from the front line and wait for them to show up in the village. You have to take up a position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And your units never conducted any sort of training in any villages; is that your position, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, we never conducted training in villages; training was conducted on training-grounds, rifle ranges, particularly-designated locations for training, if I understood your meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were schools at any moment used to deploy military equipment or weapons by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to go through all the units. I know there was an order from the corps commander and my own order to abandon all installations before the war in end 1998. If I remember correctly, there was nothing in schools almost anywhere. I may be wrong, but I'm almost certain that schools were not used.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have P1462 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is an order from the 3rd Army and it's dated 13th May 1999. General, could you read out the part right under the word "order," number 1.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Immediately relocate all Yugoslav Army commands, units, and institutions that are accommodated in schools. "Submit a report on the implementation of this order by 15 May 1999 within a regular combat report -- within a regular report." In the original it doesn't say "combat."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General if as you just stated there was no deployment of units in schools, why would the 3rd Army commander send this order out to its units?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't see to whom this was submitted, I suppose to all corps units. Perhaps -- in fact, there must have been a unit located in a schoolhouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, I don't think you answered my question really. I was asking why if, as you state, there were no -- no use of schools by the VJ, why would the 3rd Army send out such an order?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't clear enough. I tried to mentally list all my units and to remember where they were and to speak about my units. I wasn't even trying to remember where the units of the Pristina Corps or the Nis Corps were, all of them, and they were subordinated to the army command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, I didn't see you there. Was there an issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The witness's answer clarifies what I wanted to object to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, during your testimony you were shown a document regarding bombing by NATO of civilian facilities. We heard the testimony here in this court of General Naumann from -- in December of last year, who explained that because of the use by Serb forces of civilian facilities and the deployment of military equipment in civilian facilities, the task of NATO was made very difficult. These were tactics that were used by the Serb army, isn't that correct, General, deployment in civilian facilities of both troops and military equipment?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about my unit. We tried to avoid using such buildings, but the law allows us to use the premises of socially owned or privately owned businesses and companies, even privately owned companies whose premises are adequate, physically adequate, for placing army materiel, but that is no justification for targeting a civilian building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your answer, General. So you are conceding that you did use privately owned premises for military purposes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not admitting to having used them. I'm saying the law allows using all socially owned companies for the defence of the country; that is, warehouses of such companies may be used for purposes of defending the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You're a professional soldier with many years of -- a very long career in the army, aren't you, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And isn't it true that according to the regulations of Laws of War, humanitarian law, once a facility, a private facility, a civilian facility is used by the army it becomes a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if your troops - and I'm talking of the Pristina Corps - were deployed in military -- in civilian facilities and privately owned businesses, wouldn't that make such facilities legitimate military targets during a state of war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. If we had used such facilities, they would have been legitimate targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Let's move on to a different topic now. You spoke about the use of tanks by your brigade, and you said in response to questions by my learned colleague from the Defence that there was no reason to drive tanks around during the state of war. And you said -- your words were that would be crazy because they would have been destroyed by NATO, that's at page 18945 of the transcript. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember saying that. I said that -- I didn't say that tanks were moving around in open space. I said that tanks arrived and immediately took up their defence positions. They were not used for parading, they were used for defence, and they had to get into defence positions as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say they had to get into defence positions, you mean that once they got to a certain position they would remain static at that location; they would not be moved around, deployed, to other locations. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant something quite different. A unit would take up a position and engineer that position, build fortifications, et cetera. If something happens that makes this position dangerous, the unit can relocate within its own area of responsibility. The unit does not pull out the ignition key and stay there for three months. The position is not unique for every combat vehicle. There are two or three back-up positions so that if something happens, the vehicle and the unit can move to a safe place. That's the -- that's called the manoeuvre movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So were tank platoons used in operations by your units during the state of war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were used in combat and battles, not in operations. An operation is something far larger, and it was only when the units were directly threatened, when they were attacked. So they were used only for direct defence, otherwise it would have been very dangerous to move them around for combat because it would have been disastrous for the unit. The unit would have been discovered and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you use tanks to shell or provide fire support during combat actions?
